turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I ended it, and I know I needed to. But now I’m just alone with all of it. I don’t really have anyone to call.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You ended the relationship because you felt you needed to, and now you’re carrying the loneliness and everything that comes with it by yourself. I’m glad you told me. Are you thinking of ending your life? You can call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, at any time.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: No, I’m not thinking of ending my life. I’m just so tired of having nobody there. The breakup was the right choice, but I still miss having someone to talk to at the end of the day.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You’re sure ending it was right, and you still miss having someone to share the day with. That kind of loneliness can hurt. What do you miss most about those end-of-day conversations?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Just having someone who already knew all the little things. I could tell them something stupid that happened at work without having to explain everything first. Now I get home and it’s just… quiet.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You miss being known in all the small details, and having someone who understood the background without you having to start from the beginning. Then you come home to silence. What happened at work today that you wish you could’ve told them?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A customer came in with this tiny dog in a raincoat, and it kept trying to climb into my tote bag. It was ridiculous. I would’ve sent them a picture. Now I just have the picture sitting in my phone and nobody to send it to.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That sounds ridiculously cute—a tiny raincoat dog trying to claim your tote bag. It makes sense that the picture feels a little lonely sitting there when you’re used to sharing things like that. What did the dog look like?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Yellow raincoat, ears sticking out, completely determined about my bag. I still keep opening the picture like I’m going to send it to them. I don’t know. It’s such a small thing, but it’s making me sad.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: The yellow raincoat and those determined little ears sound adorable. And it isn’t silly that the picture makes you sad; it’s tied to the habit of sharing your day with someone who mattered. What do you feel when you open it, besides the sadness?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Mostly this little urge to tell them, and then I remember I can’t—or shouldn’t. I don’t want to reopen things. I just wish missing them didn’t make me question myself.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That urge to share doesn’t mean ending the relationship was the wrong choice. It can just mean you miss the familiar closeness, even while you’re trying to protect the boundary you chose. What do you find yourself questioning most?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: She broke up with me over text. I just keep thinking how gross that is. Like, I didn’t even get a real conversation.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: Getting broken up with over text can feel so cold, especially when you wanted a real conversation. No wonder you keep thinking about how unfair and hurtful it was. What’s been hitting you hardest since it happened?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And then our friends knew. A couple of them asked me about it before I’d even figured out what to say. It made me feel so exposed.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You were still trying to take it in, and suddenly other people knew and were asking you about it. That sounds really exposing, like you lost the chance to decide when and how to tell them. Did any of your friends respond in a way that felt comforting?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: One friend was decent about it. The others were just awkward, asking if I was okay like they already knew everything. I hated having to act normal.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: One friend showed you some care, but the others’ awkward questions left you feeling watched while you were still hurting. Having to act normal on top of that sounds exhausting. What do you wish you could have said to them?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I wish I could’ve said, “Stop asking me like this is gossip.” But I didn’t. I just shrugged and changed the subject.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You wanted to call out how exposed and gossiped-about you felt, but in the moment you just got through it by changing the subject. That makes sense. Do you think you might want to tell them that now, or would you rather keep some distance?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Maybe I’ll tell one of them if it comes up again. I don’t want to make a whole thing out of it. I’m just tired of everyone knowing before I’m ready.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You might say something if it comes up again, without turning it into a big confrontation. And you’re tired of people knowing before you’ve had a chance to process it—that’s a real loss of privacy. What would feel okay to say if someone brings it up again?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Maybe just, “I know you mean well, but I don’t want to talk about it right now.” That feels doable. I’m still pretty grossed out by how she handled it, though.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That sounds clear and gentle, and you don’t owe anyone more than you’re ready to share. It makes sense you’re still grossed out by how she ended things over text. What part of it keeps replaying for you most?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I just feel so embarrassed about how I look lately. My hair’s completely out of control, and I don’t want to turn my camera on.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It sounds like you’re feeling really self-conscious, especially about your hair, and turning on your camera feels like too much right now. What’s been going on that’s made this feel so hard lately?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I haven’t been able to get a haircut in ages, and it’s just… a mess. I’m getting older too, and it feels like everything’s starting to sag. I keep thinking people will notice.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It sounds like the overdue haircut is making you feel more exposed, and getting older is adding to the worry that people are judging how you look. That sounds painful. What feels hardest about other people noticing?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I guess I’m afraid they’ll see me and think I’ve let myself go. And when I’m ready to date again, I’m scared someone will look at me and just reject me.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You’re worried that people will mistake a rough patch for not caring about yourself, and that someone you like might reject you because of how you look. That’s a really tender fear. What do you wish a future date could see about you, beyond your appearance?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I’d want them to see I’m kind, and that I’m funny when I’m comfortable. But it feels like they won’t get far enough to see that if they don’t like how I look.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You want someone to get to know your kindness and humor, but you’re afraid your appearance will decide things before they get the chance. That uncertainty can feel heavy. Has anything happened recently that made that fear feel stronger?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Not one thing, really. I had a Zoom meeting yesterday and kept my camera off. Then I felt bad about that too, like I was being weird. I just don’t want people looking at me right now.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You kept your camera off because being looked at felt uncomfortable, and then you judged yourself for it. That sounds like a lot to carry. What was it like to be in the meeting with the camera off?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I could focus better, honestly. But I kept imagining everyone wondering why I wasn’t on camera. I know they probably weren’t thinking about me that much, but I still felt exposed somehow.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It sounds like having the camera off helped you focus, even while part of you worried people were noticing. That uneasy feeling can linger even when you know they may not be thinking about it much. What might help you feel a little more at ease in the next meeting?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I’m just so tired of asking my kids to do the simplest things over and over. It turns into a whole thing every time.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It sounds exhausting to repeat yourself over and over, especially when even small requests turn into a big thing. What usually happens when you ask them?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I ask them to get ready for bed, or pick up their stuff, and they just ignore me. Then I end up raising my voice, and I hate that.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You want them to listen without having to raise your voice, and then you feel bad when it turns into that. What do you notice they’re doing when they ignore you?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Usually they’re on their tablets or doing something else. I’m not sure they even hear me until I’m angry. Then suddenly I’m the bad guy.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: That sounds really frustrating: you feel ignored until you get angry, and then the focus shifts to your reaction. What feels hardest about that moment for you?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I guess it’s feeling like I have to get angry to matter. I don’t want to be that parent, but I don’t know how else to get through to them.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It hurts to feel like anger is the only way they hear you, especially when that’s not the kind of parent you want to be. How old are your kids?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: They’re 8 and 11. The older one especially just shuts me out, and then the younger one copies him. I feel like I’m losing control of the whole evening.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: With an 8- and 11-year-old, it can feel like one tuning you out sets the tone for the whole evening. Losing control of that routine sounds overwhelming. What part of bedtime tends to unravel first?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The tablets, mostly. I say it’s time to turn them off and they ask for five more minutes, then argue when I say no. By then I’m already tense.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: The five-more-minutes request and arguing leave you tense before bedtime has even really started. Would it help to think together about a calmer way to handle the tablet transition?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I need a job, but almost everything I find wants weekends. And there aren’t any day cares around here that take kids on weekends. I don’t know what I’m supposed to do.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You need work, but the weekend hours clash with the lack of childcare nearby, and it sounds like you’re feeling stuck. That’s a really hard bind. What kind of work or schedule would be possible for you?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Weekdays would be possible. I just keep finding jobs that want me to be available weekends too, even if the shifts are mostly during the week.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You’re finding weekday shifts, but employers still want weekend availability, so childcare keeps getting in the way. That sounds frustrating. Have you had a chance to tell any employers you’re available weekdays but not weekends?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A couple times. They usually say weekends are part of the job, so I don’t even get an interview. I can’t really afford to keep applying and getting nowhere.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You’ve been clear about your weekday availability, and being turned down before you even get an interview is wearing you down. It makes sense that applying feels costly when it keeps going nowhere. Would it help to look together at jobs that are more often weekday-only, or at ways to screen openings before spending time on them?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Maybe. I just don’t know what jobs are actually weekday-only around here. I’ve mostly been looking at retail and food service because that’s what I’ve done before.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: Retail and food service are familiar, but their weekend requirements are blocking you. Some people find weekday hours more often in places like school cafeterias, office cleaning, warehouses, or reception and data-entry work, though it varies by area. What kind of work have you done before?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Mostly cashiering and serving. I don’t have much office experience, so I’m not sure anyone would hire me for that. School cafeteria sounds like it might fit, but I’d need to know if they’re hiring.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: Cashiering and serving give you useful customer-service experience, and a school cafeteria could fit your schedule—but you’d need a real opening to pursue. What town or area are you in? I can help you think of places to check.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I’d rather not share exactly where I live. It’s a small area, and I’m not sure there are even school cafeteria jobs nearby. I could check the school district website, I guess.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You don’t need to share where you live. Checking the school district’s jobs page sounds like a good, low-effort place to start; you could also call the district office and ask whether cafeteria roles are posted there or through a food-service contractor. Would you like help wording a quick call or message?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I’m applying for a job I don’t think I’m qualified for. I keep telling myself there’s no point, but I can’t stop thinking about it.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: Part of you thinks there’s no point, and another part keeps coming back to the job. What feels most compelling about it?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It’s the kind of work I’ve wanted to do for years. But when I look at the requirements, I feel like I’m already behind everyone else. I’m so tired of feeling like I’ll never be good enough.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You’ve wanted this kind of work for years, and the requirements are making you feel like you’re already too far behind. That sounds exhausting. Would it help to look at what you do bring to the role, alongside the gaps?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I don’t know. I’m having a hard time even thinking about it without feeling worse. I just feel so low lately, and this job thing is making me feel like I’ve failed at everything.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It sounds like this job is landing on top of a deeper feeling that you’ve failed at everything. I’m glad you told me. Are you thinking of ending your life? You can call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, at any time.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: No, I’m not thinking about ending my life. I just feel stuck and ashamed, like I should be further along by now. I don’t really know what to do with that.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: I’m glad you’re not thinking about ending your life, and I hear how stuck and ashamed you feel about where you are right now. You don’t have to solve the job question this minute. What’s been weighing on you most lately?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Mostly the feeling that everyone else is moving forward and I’m just… not. I keep thinking if I can’t even get this job, then maybe I’m not going anywhere.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It sounds like this one job has started to feel like a verdict on your whole future, while everyone else seems to be moving ahead. That’s a heavy thing to carry. Since these feelings have been weighing on you, talking with a counsellor could help, and I’m here with you too. What’s one thing you wish someone understood about how this has felt?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I wish someone understood how much effort it takes just to keep trying. From the outside it probably looks like I’m being lazy or indecisive, but I’m really scared of putting myself out there and getting proof that I’m not good enough.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It takes a lot of effort to keep trying when each step feels like it could confirm your worst fear. That doesn’t sound lazy; it sounds frightening and exhausting. You don’t have to decide about the application right now. Would it feel okay to tell me what part of putting yourself out there scares you most?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I don’t really know where to start. I’ve just been feeling low for a while.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It sounds like you’ve been carrying a low feeling for a while, and it’s hard to know where to begin. I’m glad you told me. What has this been like for you lately?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Since my dad died, everything feels like it’s just kept getting harder. I’m trying to look after my mum, and now we have to move. I’m so tired, and I don’t know how to make things better.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: Losing your dad, caring for your mum, and facing a move all at once sounds like an enormous amount to carry. It makes sense that you feel so tired. What feels heaviest right now?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Probably the move. We lost his income, and I’ve been out of work, so I don’t know where we’ll end up. And with both of us being high risk for COVID, everything feels more complicated. I just feel stuck.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You’re facing housing and money worries while trying to keep you and your mum safe, and it feels like there’s no clear way forward. That’s a lot to hold. What’s the most urgent part of the move right now?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I think finding somewhere we can afford. I don’t even know where to look, and I don’t have much energy to deal with calls and forms. My mum depends on me, and I feel guilty that I can’t sort it all out.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You’re trying to find affordable housing while grieving and caring for your mum, and feeling guilty because you’re exhausted. That doesn’t mean you’re letting her down; you’re carrying a lot. Would it help to look at one small next step together, like finding a local housing or benefits adviser who can help with the calls and forms?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Maybe. I’m not sure I have the energy to start contacting people, but having someone help with the forms would take some pressure off. I just don’t know who to ask.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It sounds like help with the paperwork could ease some pressure, even if reaching out feels hard right now. A local council housing team, a community advice service, or a social worker may be able to point you to someone who helps with forms. What country or area are you in?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We’re in the UK. I could maybe try the council, but even thinking about another call is overwhelming. I wish someone could just tell me where to begin.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You’re willing to try the council, but even making the call feels like too much. A low-effort first step could be visiting your council’s website and searching “housing options” or “homelessness prevention”; many councils have an online form or email option. If you’d rather have someone help you work out what to ask, Citizens Advice can point you toward local support.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I just miss being able to see my family and friends. It feels like every day is the same now.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You miss seeing the people you care about, and the days are starting to blur together. That sounds lonely. What do you miss most about being with them?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Just the ordinary stuff, I guess. Having dinner together, dropping by without planning it. I didn’t realize how much I needed that.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: It’s the small, unplanned moments you’re missing—the shared meals and being able to just stop by. It makes sense that those feel important now. Is there someone you’d like to have a little ordinary time with soon?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My sister, probably. We text, but it’s not the same. I keep thinking I should call her, then I just don’t have the energy.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You miss the closeness of seeing your sister, and even calling feels like a lot when your energy is low. Would a short voice message feel easier than a call?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Maybe. I could probably send her a voice message. I just feel kind of flat most days, though. It’s not only missing people.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: Feeling flat most days sounds heavy, especially when it’s more than just missing people. Since it’s been affecting how you feel day to day, talking with a counsellor or doctor could help. How long have you been feeling this way?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A few weeks, I think. Some days are okay, but mostly I just don’t feel like doing much. I haven’t really told anyone that part.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: I’m glad you told me. A few weeks of feeling flat and not wanting to do much sounds hard to carry quietly. Is there someone you trust, like your sister, you might tell a little of this to?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Maybe I could tell my sister. I don’t want to make her worry, but I’m tired of pretending I’m fine.

turns.speaker: helper
turns.text: You’re tired of pretending, and you’re worried that being honest might make your sister worry. You could keep it simple, like, “I’ve been feeling flat lately, and I don’t need you to fix it—I just wanted you to know.” Would it feel okay to send her that?
